Testably.Abstractions provides injectable abstractions for the static parts of the .NET base class library (BCL), namely the file system, time and randomness, with feature-complete in-memory mocks for tests.

Depend on IFileSystem, ITimeSystem and IRandomSystem in production. Swap in the in-memory mocks for tests: deterministic, cross-platform, no temp folders or Thread.Sleep. File system Time system Random system CatalogService.cs public class CatalogService(IFileSystem fileSystem) { public void Export(string json) { fileSystem.Directory.CreateDirectory("exports"); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("exports/catalog.json", json); } } CatalogServiceTests.cs [Test] public async Task Export_WritesCatalogToExportsFolder() { MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); CatalogService sut = new(fileSystem); sut.Export("""{ "title": "Red Square" }"""); await That(fileSystem.File.ReadAllText("exports/catalog.json")) .IsEqualTo("""{ "title": "Red Square" }"""); } Exhibition.cs public class Exhibition(ITimeSystem timeSystem, DateTime closesAt) { public bool IsOpen => timeSystem.DateTime.UtcNow < closesAt; } ExhibitionTests.cs [Test] public async Task IsOpen_ReturnsFalse_AfterClosingDate() { MockTimeSystem timeSystem = new(new DateTime(2026, 3, 1, 0, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc)); Exhibition sut = new(timeSystem, closesAt: new DateTime(2026, 4, 15, 0, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc)); timeSystem.TimeProvider.AdvanceBy(TimeSpan.FromDays(60)); await That(sut.IsOpen).IsFalse(); } ArtworkOfTheDay.cs public class ArtworkOfTheDay(IRandomSystem randomSystem, string[] artworks) { public string Pick() => artworks[randomSystem.Random.Shared.Next(artworks.Length)]; } ArtworkOfTheDayTests.cs [Test] public async Task Pick_ReturnsTheArtworkAtTheRandomIndex() { MockRandomSystem randomSystem = new(RandomProvider.Generate(intGenerator: 1)); ArtworkOfTheDay sut = new(randomSystem, ["Red Square", "Blue Circles", "Yellow Lines"]); await That(sut.Pick()).IsEqualTo("Blue Circles"); }

Testably.Abstractions shares the IFileSystem interface with TestableIO.System.IO.Abstractions, so your production code does not change when you switch testing libraries. What you get on top: Advanced testing scenarios: FileSystemWatcher, SafeFileHandle, multiple drives with size limits. Cross-platform simulation: run a Linux file system on Windows (and vice versa) to exercise platform-specific behavior from a single CI job. A second abstraction layer for time and randomness. Version 8 adds support for .NET 11: the packages target net11.0, and the mocks and the compression package implement the new .NET 11 APIs. Version 8 of Testably.Abstractions.Testing also replaces the extension point interfaces of the mocks with classes, so that they can grow without breaking every implementer, and changes how MockTimeSystem fires timers. Tests that only use the mocks without custom strategies and without timers need no changes.

The interfaces mirror the new .NET 11 APIs, and the mocks implement them: Random system: IRandom.NextInteger<T>(), NextInteger<T>(T), NextInteger<T>(T, T) and NextBinaryFloat<T>(). RandomMock uses its configured generators for int, long, float and double. Hard links: IFile.CreateHardLink and IFileInfo.CreateAsHardLink. In MockFileSystem, all links of a file share its content, attributes, timestamps and Unix file mode. FileShare locks apply to the file, so opening one link without sharing blocks the others, and the content and drive space are only released when the last link is deleted. Null handles: IFile.OpenNullHandle returns a handle that discards written bytes and returns no data. Like the real handle, it only supports seeking on Linux and macOS. Compression: IZipArchive.CreateEntry, CreateEntryFromFile and CreateEntryFromFileAsync with a password and a ZipEncryptionMethod; ExtractToDirectory(Async) and ExtractToFile(Async) with ZipExtractionOptions; IZipFile.CreateFromDirectory(Async) with ZipFileCreationOptions; IZipArchiveEntry.Open(Async) with a FileAccess and/or a password, and the properties CompressionMethod, EncryptionMethod and VersionMadeBy. MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("original.txt", "foo"); fileSystem.File.CreateHardLink("link.txt", "original.txt"); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("original.txt", "bar"); await That(fileSystem.File.ReadAllText("link.txt")).IsEqualTo("bar");

On net11.0, the mocks follow these behavior changes of the .NET 11 runtime: IFileInfo.Open, OpenRead, OpenWrite and OpenText refresh the cached state of the IFileInfo, like Create already did (dotnet/runtime#124429). On Linux and macOS, file streams are never asynchronous, because Unix opens regular files without O_NONBLOCK (breaking change, dotnet/runtime#125220). A stream created from a handle follows the handle and ignores the isAsync argument (breaking change). On Linux and macOS, CreateHardLink with a missing target throws a DirectoryNotFoundException when the link path has no directory part (dotnet/runtime#120041). On Linux and macOS, ITimer.Dispose(WaitHandle) with a Mutex or Semaphore disposes the timer and then throws an InvalidOperationException.

The strategy interfaces of MockFileSystem are replaced with abstract base classes. A custom strategy derives from the base class and overrides its members instead of implementing an interface. v7 v8 IAccessControlStrategy AccessControlStrategy IUnixFileModeStrategy UnixFileModeStrategy ISafeFileHandleStrategy SafeFileHandleStrategy WithAccessControlStrategy, WithUnixFileModeStrategy and WithSafeFileHandleStrategy take the base classes. The built-in strategies (DefaultAccessControlStrategy, DefaultSafeFileHandleStrategy, NullSafeFileHandleStrategy and NullUnixFileModeStrategy) work unchanged.

documents.t: AccessControlStrategy no longer has the IsAccessGranted(fullPath, extensibility) overload without the AccessRequest, and DefaultAccessControlStrategy no longer has the constructor with a two-argument callback. Add the AccessRequest parameter to the callback: // v7 new DefaultAccessControlStrategy((path, extensibility) => !path.EndsWith(".lock")); // v8 new DefaultAccessControlStrategy((path, extensibility, _) => !path.EndsWith(".lock"));

UnixFileModeStrategy.IsAccessGranted receives an AccessRequest instead of the requested FileAccess; read it from request.Access. OnSetUnixFileMode is virtual and does nothing by default, so only override it when you need it. // v7 public class MyStrategy : IUnixFileModeStrategy { public bool IsAccessGranted(string fullPath, IFileSystemExtensibility extensibility, UnixFileMode mode, FileAccess requestedAccess) => requestedAccess == FileAccess.Read || mode.HasFlag(UnixFileMode.UserWrite); public void OnSetUnixFileMode(string fullPath, IFileSystemExtensibility extensibility, UnixFileMode mode) { } } // v8 public class MyStrategy : UnixFileModeStrategy { public override bool IsAccessGranted(string fullPath, IFileSystemExtensibility extensibility, UnixFileMode mode, AccessRequest request) => request.Access == FileAccess.Read || mode.HasFlag(UnixFileMode.UserWrite); } See access control, Unix file mode and safe file handles.

ITimerStrategy is removed, and TimerStrategy is a sealed class. MockTimeSystem.WithTimerStrategy takes a TimerStrategy and TimerStrategy.Default returns one. Replace references to ITimerStrategy with TimerStrategy. Code that creates a strategy with new TimerStrategy(...) keeps working unchanged; a custom implementation of ITimerStrategy creates a TimerStrategy with the same TimerMode and swallowExceptions setting instead.

MockTimeSystem fires due timers in the order of their due time, with the clock at their due time, and no longer lets timeouts move the clock. Check tests that use timers or auto-advance for the following changes: A timer callback sees its own due time instead of the final time of an advance. With auto-advance, a one-shot timer whose state is a CancellationTokenSource is a timeout and no longer moves the clock on its own. This includes the timers of new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan, TimeProvider) and Task.WaitAsync(TimeSpan, TimeProvider) on ToTimeProvider(). Code that waits for nothing but a timeout, e.g. Task.Delay(Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan, timeProvider, cts.Token), waits until something else moves the clock. Move the clock with AdvanceBy or give such a timer a different state. With auto-advance, parallel Thread.Sleep and Task.Delay waits overlap like real ones instead of adding up: two parallel one-second sleeps move the clock by one second, not two. Explicit AdvanceBy calls still add up. Task.Delay returns a canceled task for a canceled token instead of throwing, like the real one. Await the task to observe the OperationCanceledException. See auto-advance and timers.

Testably.Abstractions ships three optional NuGet packages that extend IFileSystem with capabilities the base class library (BCL) keeps in separate namespaces. Package Adds to IFileSystem Testably.Abstractions.Compression ZipFile and ZipArchive extension properties Testably.Abstractions.AccessControl GetAccessControl / SetAccessControl on files and directories Testably.Abstractions.MemoryMappedFiles MemoryMappedFile extension property All packages target the IFileSystem interface, so they work transparently against either RealFileSystem or MockFileSystem.
Implements the methods from FileSystemAclExtensions on the IFileSystem interface so production code that reads or writes ACLs works against both real and mocked file systems.

.NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package Testably.Abstractions.AccessControl <PackageReference Include="Testably.Abstractions.AccessControl" Version="7.2.0" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="Testably.Abstractions.AccessControl" Version="7.2.0" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="Testably.Abstractions.AccessControl" /> Latest version: 7.2.0 The extensions live in the Testably.Abstractions namespace.

Extension on Methods IDirectory CreateDirectory(path, DirectorySecurity), GetAccessControl, SetAccessControl IDirectoryInfo Create(DirectorySecurity), GetAccessControl, SetAccessControl IFile GetAccessControl, SetAccessControl IFileInfo GetAccessControl, SetAccessControl FileSystemStream GetAccessControl, SetAccessControl Each GetAccessControl overload accepts an optional AccessControlSections mask, matching the BCL. IFileSystem fileSystem; // injected DirectorySecurity acl = fileSystem.Directory.GetAccessControl("archive"); fileSystem.Directory.SetAccessControl("vault", acl); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("provenance.txt", ""); FileSecurity fileAcl = fileSystem.File.GetAccessControl("provenance.txt");

On RealFileSystem the calls forward to System.IO.FileSystemAclExtensions. On MockFileSystem the ACL object is stored as metadata via IFileSystemExtensibility and round-tripped: set it, read it back, and it will be the same object. The mock does not enforce the stored ACL. To simulate denied access, combine the package with MockFileSystem.WithAccessControlStrategy(...). Windows-only All ACL APIs are marked [SupportedOSPlatform("windows")]. Calling them on Linux/macOS throws PlatformNotSupportedException.
Wraps System.IO.Compression.ZipFile and System.IO.Compression.ZipArchive as extensions on IFileSystem.

.NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package Testably.Abstractions.Compression <PackageReference Include="Testably.Abstractions.Compression" Version="7.2.0" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="Testably.Abstractions.Compression" Version="7.2.0" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="Testably.Abstractions.Compression" /> Latest version: 7.2.0 The extensions live in the Testably.Abstractions namespace.

System.IO.Compression.ZipFile operates on real string paths and System.IO.Compression.ZipArchive operates on Streams; neither knows about IFileSystem. The package bridges the two: // With Testably.Abstractions.Compression, one line: fileSystem.ZipFile.CreateFromDirectory("artworks", "artworks.zip"); Without the companion package (~15 lines of glue) using MemoryStream buffer = new(); using (ZipArchive archive = new(buffer, ZipArchiveMode.Create, leaveOpen: true)) { AddDirectory("", "artworks"); void AddDirectory(string prefix, string directory) { foreach (string file in fileSystem.Directory.GetFiles(directory)) { ZipArchiveEntry entry = archive.CreateEntry(prefix + Path.GetFileName(file)); using Stream entryStream = entry.Open(); entryStream.Write(fileSystem.File.ReadAllBytes(file)); } foreach (string sub in fileSystem.Directory.GetDirectories(directory)) { string name = fileSystem.Path.GetFileName(sub); archive.CreateEntry(prefix + name + "/"); AddDirectory(prefix + name + "/", sub); } } } buffer.Position = 0; using FileSystemStream output = fileSystem.File.Create("artworks.zip"); buffer.CopyTo(output); Extraction looks similar: open a ZipArchive in Read mode, loop the entries, recreate directories on the file system, copy each entry's stream into fileSystem.File.WriteAllBytes. The package replaces this glue with a one-line call. Beyond brevity, it also gives you stream/path overloads on both sides, async variants on .NET 10+, and an IZipArchive / IZipArchiveEntry wrapper so the abstraction extends through the archive itself rather than stopping at the zip boundary. Production uses the real implementation On RealFileSystem, every call forwards to the matching System.IO.Compression method, so production code keeps the performance of the base class library (BCL). Only MockFileSystem uses an in-memory implementation.

fileSystem.ZipFile exposes the static methods of System.IO.Compression.ZipFile: fileSystem.ZipFile .CreateFromDirectory("artworks", "artworks.zip"); fileSystem.ZipFile .ExtractToDirectory("artworks.zip", "vault"); using IZipArchive archive = fileSystem.ZipFile .Open("artworks.zip", ZipArchiveMode.Update); All overloads from the BCL are present, including the async variants on .NET 10+ (CreateFromDirectoryAsync, ExtractToDirectoryAsync, OpenAsync, OpenReadAsync) and, on .NET 11+, the overloads that take ZipFileCreationOptions or ZipExtractionOptions to create and extract password-protected archives.

fileSystem.ZipArchive is a factory for IZipArchive from a Stream (matches the new ZipArchive(...) constructors): using FileSystemStream stream = fileSystem.File.OpenRead("artworks.zip"); using IZipArchive archive = fileSystem.ZipArchive .New(stream, ZipArchiveMode.Read); foreach (IZipArchiveEntry entry in archive.Entries) { Console.WriteLine(entry.FullName); } IZipArchive exposes Entries, Mode, CreateEntry, CreateEntryFromFile, GetEntry, ExtractToDirectory and, on .NET 10+, the async counterparts CreateEntryFromFileAsync and ExtractToDirectoryAsync. On .NET 11+ the create methods also accept a password and a ZipEncryptionMethod, and the extract methods accept ZipExtractionOptions. IZipArchiveEntry mirrors ZipArchiveEntry (Open, Delete, LastWriteTime, Length, CompressedLength, …), including the .NET 11+ members CompressionMethod, EncryptionMethod, VersionMadeBy and the Open overloads with a FileAccess or a password.
Wraps System.IO.MemoryMappedFiles.MemoryMappedFile as a MemoryMappedFile extension property on IFileSystem, so memory-mapped-file code can be tested against the in-memory MockFileSystem.

.NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package Testably.Abstractions.MemoryMappedFiles <PackageReference Include="Testably.Abstractions.MemoryMappedFiles" Version="7.2.0" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="Testably.Abstractions.MemoryMappedFiles" Version="7.2.0" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="Testably.Abstractions.MemoryMappedFiles" /> Latest version: 7.2.0 The extensions live in the Testably.Abstractions namespace.

System.IO.MemoryMappedFiles.MemoryMappedFile.CreateFromFile needs a real path (or a real FileStream) on disk; it cannot map a file that only exists inside a MockFileSystem. Without the companion package, any production code that touches MemoryMappedFile is effectively untestable against the mock: your test either falls back to writing real temp files or the memory-mapped path stays uncovered. IFileSystem fileSystem = //... using IMemoryMappedFile mappedFile = fileSystem.MemoryMappedFile .CreateFromFile("red-square.png"); using IMemoryMappedViewAccessor accessor = mappedFile.CreateViewAccessor(); accessor.Write(0, 42); int value = accessor.ReadInt32(0); The same code runs unchanged against RealFileSystem and MockFileSystem. Production uses the real implementation On RealFileSystem, every call forwards to the base class library (BCL) MemoryMappedFile, so production keeps the native memory-mapping semantics. Only on MockFileSystem are the views built over the in-memory file bytes.

fileSystem.MemoryMappedFile exposes the CreateFromFile overloads of System.IO.MemoryMappedFiles.MemoryMappedFile: using IMemoryMappedFile fromPath = fileSystem.MemoryMappedFile .CreateFromFile("red-square.png", FileMode.Open, mapName: null, capacity: 0, MemoryMappedFileAccess.ReadWrite); The FileStream-based overload is exposed with a FileSystemStream instead of a FileStream, so it works against both the real and the mocked file system: using FileSystemStream stream = fileSystem.FileStream.New("red-square.png", FileMode.Open, FileAccess.ReadWrite); using IMemoryMappedFile mappedFile = fileSystem.MemoryMappedFile.CreateFromFile( stream, mapName: null, capacity: 0, MemoryMappedFileAccess.ReadWrite, HandleInheritability.None, leaveOpen: true);

An IMemoryMappedFile creates two kinds of views over its bytes, mirroring the BCL: // Random-access, typed reads and writes: using IMemoryMappedViewAccessor accessor = mappedFile.CreateViewAccessor(0, 100); accessor.Write(0, 1234567); int roundtrip = accessor.ReadInt32(0); // A Stream over a window of the mapped bytes: using MemoryMappedFileSystemViewStream stream = mappedFile.CreateViewStream(0, 50); stream.Write([1, 2, 3, 4], 0, 4); IMemoryMappedViewAccessor mirrors MemoryMappedViewAccessor: the primitive Read*/Write overloads, the generic Read<T>/Write<T> for structs, ReadArray<T>/WriteArray<T>, plus Capacity, CanRead, CanWrite, PointerOffset and Flush. MemoryMappedFileSystemViewStream derives from UnmanagedMemoryStream, like the real MemoryMappedViewStream, and adds its Capacity and PointerOffset members.

On MockFileSystem the reads and writes, the capacity handling and the thrown exceptions mirror the real MemoryMappedViewAccessor / MemoryMappedViewStream, including: Default view access is ReadWrite: creating a writable view over a read-only mapping throws UnauthorizedAccessException, exactly as the BCL does. The file and its views have independent lifetimes: a view stays usable after the IMemoryMappedFile is disposed. CopyOnWrite views privatize pages on write: their writes are neither persisted nor visible to other views, while pages they have not written keep reflecting changes made through other views.

These parts of the BCL operate on operating-system shared memory rather than a file. They forward normally on RealFileSystem, but throw NotSupportedException on MockFileSystem: CreateNew CreateOrOpen (Windows-only) OpenExisting (Windows-only) A non-null mapName in CreateFromFile (named mappings are shared-memory objects) The SafeMemoryMappedFileHandle / SafeMemoryMappedViewHandle handle and pointer APIs, and the SafeFileHandle-based CreateFromFile overload, are not exposed at all. The unsafe PositionPointer of a view stream throws ObjectDisposedException, because no unmanaged memory backs it.

Details tied to operating-system memory mapping that the mock simplifies View size: a view created without an explicit size has a Capacity of exactly the remaining bytes (the real file system rounds up to the page size), and PointerOffset is always 0. Visibility of writes: writes are immediately visible to all views of the same mapping, but reach the underlying file (and other streams of it) only through the backing stream, at the latest when a view is flushed or disposed. The real operating system makes them visible to other readers immediately. Disposed backing stream: when the stream passed to CreateFromFile with leaveOpen: true is disposed while views are open, operations on those views throw ObjectDisposedException. Real views keep working. Truncation: truncating the backing stream while views are open succeeds, and reads of the truncated range return zeros. The real operating system rejects the truncation. Size: the mock keeps the whole file in memory, so a memory-mapped file is limited to 2 GB. Growing it beyond that throws NotSupportedException. Exceptions: exception types and messages follow the Windows behavior of the BCL, also on Linux and macOS and for every simulated operating system. Struct size on .NET Framework: Read<T>/Write<T>/ReadArray<T>/WriteArray<T> size structs by their managed layout, like .NET (Core). The .NET Framework uses the marshalled size, so the two disagree for structs such as one containing a bool.

documents.t: When an exhibition closes, the gallery moves its artworks into the vault. The ExhibitionArchiver below does that, and depends on all three abstractions: IFileSystem to move the exhibition folder and write a note, ITimeSystem to decide whether the exhibition has closed, IRandomSystem to generate the archive number. ExhibitionArchiver.cs public record Exhibition(string Folder, DateTime ClosesAt); public class ExhibitionArchiver( IFileSystem fileSystem, ITimeSystem timeSystem, IRandomSystem randomSystem) { public string? ArchiveIfClosed(Exhibition exhibition) { if (timeSystem.DateTime.UtcNow < exhibition.ClosesAt) { return null; } string archiveNumber = randomSystem.Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N").Substring(0, 8); string target = fileSystem.Path.Combine("vault", archiveNumber); fileSystem.Directory.CreateDirectory("vault"); fileSystem.Directory.Move(exhibition.Folder, target); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText(fileSystem.Path.Combine(target, "archived-at.txt"), timeSystem.DateTime.UtcNow.ToString("O")); return archiveNumber; } } In production, register RealFileSystem, RealTimeSystem and RealRandomSystem as shown in Getting started.

The test class creates one mock of each system. The time system starts on the closing day of the exhibition, the random system returns a fixed Guid, and the file system contains the exhibition with two artworks: ExhibitionArchiverTests.cs public class ExhibitionArchiverTests { private static readonly DateTime ClosingDay = new(2026, 4, 15, 18, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc); private readonly MockFileSystem _fileSystem; private readonly MockTimeSystem _timeSystem; private readonly ExhibitionArchiver _sut; private readonly Exhibition _exhibition = new("squares", ClosingDay); public ExhibitionArchiverTests() { _timeSystem = new MockTimeSystem(ClosingDay.AddHours(-1)); _fileSystem = new MockFileSystem(o => o.UseTimeSystem(_timeSystem)); _fileSystem.Initialize() .WithSubdirectory("squares").Initialized(d => d .WithFile("red-square.png") .WithFile("yellow-square.png")); MockRandomSystem randomSystem = new(RandomProvider.Generate( guidGenerator: Guid.Parse("a1b2c3d4-0000-0000-0000-000000000000"))); _sut = new ExhibitionArchiver(_fileSystem, _timeSystem, randomSystem); } [Test] public async Task ArchiveIfClosed_WhileOpen_ShouldNotTouchTheFileSystem() { string? archiveNumber = _sut.ArchiveIfClosed(_exhibition); await That(archiveNumber).IsNull(); await That(_fileSystem.Statistics.TotalCount).IsEqualTo(0) .Because("seeding with Initialize() is not recorded in the statistics"); } [Test] public async Task ArchiveIfClosed_AfterClosing_ShouldMoveTheArtworksIntoTheVault() { _timeSystem.TimeProvider.AdvanceBy(TimeSpan.FromHours(2)); string? archiveNumber = _sut.ArchiveIfClosed(_exhibition); await That(archiveNumber).IsEqualTo("a1b2c3d4"); await That(_fileSystem.Directory.Exists("squares")).IsFalse(); await That(_fileSystem.Directory.GetFiles("vault/a1b2c3d4").Select(Path.GetFileName)) .IsEqualTo(new[] { "archived-at.txt", "red-square.png", "yellow-square.png" }).InAnyOrder(); await That(_fileSystem.File.ReadAllText("vault/a1b2c3d4/archived-at.txt")) .IsEqualTo("2026-04-15T19:00:00.0000000Z"); } [Test] public async Task ArchiveIfClosed_WhenTheVaultIsFull_ShouldKeepTheExhibition() { _timeSystem.TimeProvider.AdvanceBy(TimeSpan.FromHours(2)); _fileSystem.Intercept.Creating(FileSystemTypes.Directory, _ => throw new IOException("The vault is full.")); void Act() => _sut.ArchiveIfClosed(_exhibition); await That(Act).Throws<IOException>().WithMessage("The vault is full."); await That(_fileSystem.Directory.GetFiles("squares")).HasCount(2); } } What each mock contributes: Time system: the test starts an hour before closing and moves the clock with AdvanceBy, instead of waiting or depending on today's date. The MockFileSystem shares the same clock via UseTimeSystem, so file timestamps match the simulated time. Random system: the fixed Guid makes the archive number predictable, so the test can assert the exact target folder. File system: Initialize() seeds the exhibition, Statistics proves that nothing happened while the exhibition was open, and Intercept simulates a full vault without filling a real disk.

IFileSystem abstracts away every I/O type from System.IO so you can inject and replace it. The interface is API-compatible with TestableIO.System.IO.Abstractions: production code written against one library works with the other.

Static / new in System.IO IFileSystem member File.ReadAllText("catalog.json") fileSystem.File.ReadAllText("catalog.json") Directory.CreateDirectory("vault") fileSystem.Directory.CreateDirectory("vault") Path.Combine("vault", "red-square.png") fileSystem.Path.Combine("vault", "red-square.png") new FileInfo("catalog.json") fileSystem.FileInfo.New("catalog.json") new DirectoryInfo("vault") fileSystem.DirectoryInfo.New("vault") new FileStream(...) fileSystem.FileStream.New(...) new FileSystemWatcher(...) fileSystem.FileSystemWatcher.New(...) DriveInfo.GetDrives() fileSystem.DriveInfo.GetDrives() FileVersionInfo.GetVersionInfo(...) fileSystem.FileVersionInfo.GetVersionInfo(...) Static methods stay static on the sub-properties; constructors become factory methods (New). Everything else mirrors the framework one-to-one.

documents.t: Type Package Use it for RealFileSystem Testably.Abstractions Production MockFileSystem Testably.Abstractions.Testing Unit tests MockFileSystem is the in-memory implementation of IFileSystem shipped in Testably.Abstractions.Testing. It implements every member of IFileSystem and is exercised by the same test suite as RealFileSystem: if a test passes against the real file system, it passes against the mock, and vice versa. IFileSystem fileSystem = new MockFileSystem(); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("red-square.txt", "Oil on canvas"); string content = fileSystem.File.ReadAllText("red-square.txt"); // "Oil on canvas"

MockFileSystem accepts an options builder (MockFileSystemOptions): MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(o => o .UseCurrentDirectory("/gallery") // sets CurrentDirectory to "/gallery" .UseTimeSystem(timeSystem) // share an existing MockTimeSystem .UseRandomProvider(randomProvider) // share an existing IRandomProvider .SimulatingOperatingSystem(SimulationMode.Linux)); // simulate Linux semantics UseCurrentDirectory() (no argument) seeds the mock with the host's actual working directory, useful when test code uses relative paths and you want them to resolve against the same place the real system would. The mock also exposes MockFileSystem.TimeSystem and MockFileSystem.RandomSystem if you didn't wire them in yourself. Use them to assert against the same instances the file system is using internally.

To simulate Windows access control list (ACL) restrictions, register an AccessControlStrategy with WithAccessControlStrategy(...). The built-in DefaultAccessControlStrategy takes a callback (fullPath, extensibility, request) => bool; return false to deny access to that path. Operations on a denied path then throw UnauthorizedAccessException with the message "Access to the path '{fullPath}' is denied.", like the real Windows file system: MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.WithAccessControlStrategy( new DefaultAccessControlStrategy((path, _, _) => !path.EndsWith("provenance.txt"))); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("catalog.json", "[]"); // ok fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("provenance.txt", ""); // throws UnauthorizedAccessException The AccessRequest describes the requested access, so you can simulate files and directories that can be read but not written, or written but not deleted: Access is the requested FileAccess. Enumerating a directory requests FileAccess.Read. As FileAccess is a flags enum, use HasFlag to also cover FileAccess.ReadWrite. IsDelete is true when the file or directory is deleted. A delete also requests FileAccess.Write. MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("catalog.json", "[]"); fileSystem.WithAccessControlStrategy( new DefaultAccessControlStrategy((path, _, request) => !(path.EndsWith("catalog.json") && request.Access.HasFlag(FileAccess.Write)))); fileSystem.File.ReadAllText("catalog.json"); // ok fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("catalog.json", "[]"); // throws UnauthorizedAccessException For a custom strategy, derive from the abstract AccessControlStrategy base class and override IsAccessGranted. Windows-only WithAccessControlStrategy throws PlatformNotSupportedException on non-Windows hosts (and when simulating a non-Windows OS). ACL functionality is intentionally tied to Windows behavior.

This page is about denying access. To read and write FileSecurity / DirectorySecurity objects (the GetAccessControl / SetAccessControl APIs), install the Testably.Abstractions.AccessControl companion package.

MockFileSystem supports multiple drives with independent quotas. This is most useful when simulating Windows, where drive letters carry meaning, but the main drive can also be configured on non-Windows hosts.

MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem .WithDrive("D:", d => d.SetTotalSize(1024 * 1024)) // 1 MiB total .InitializeIn("D:") .WithFile("inventory.txt") .WithSubdirectory("vault").Initialized(s => s .WithAFile(".json").Which( f => f.HasStringContent("{\"artworks\":1}"))); This adds a D: drive limited to 1 MiB and seeds it with an empty inventory.txt and a vault sub-directory containing one randomly named JSON file.

WithDrive without an argument configures the default drive (works on any OS): MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.WithDrive(d => d.SetTotalSize(20)); // Throws IOException: not enough space on the disk fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("catalog.txt", "a catalogue longer than 20 bytes"); When a drive runs out of space, every file operation that writes content throws IOException, exactly as on the real system. AvailableFreeSpace tracks every byte written, appended or freed: MockFileSystem fileSystem = new MockFileSystem() .WithDrive(d => d.SetTotalSize(100)); IDriveInfo drive = fileSystem.GetDefaultDrive(); await That(drive.AvailableFreeSpace).IsEqualTo(100); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("catalog.txt", "A catalogue entry of 29 bytes"); await That(drive.AvailableFreeSpace).IsEqualTo(71); fileSystem.File.AppendAllText("catalog.txt", "And 17 more bytes"); await That(drive.AvailableFreeSpace).IsEqualTo(54); void WriteTooMuch() => fileSystem.File.WriteAllBytes("red-square.png", new byte[90]); await That(WriteTooMuch).Throws<IOException>(); await That(drive.AvailableFreeSpace).IsEqualTo(54) .Because("the failed write did not consume space"); fileSystem.File.Delete("catalog.txt"); await That(drive.AvailableFreeSpace).IsEqualTo(100);

WithUncDrive("server") registers a Universal Naming Convention (UNC) server, so paths like \\server\share\... resolve in the mock. Like a local drive, it starts empty, so create the share directory before writing into it: MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.WithUncDrive("build-server"); fileSystem.Directory.CreateDirectory("//build-server/share"); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("//build-server/share/catalog.json", "[]"); IDriveInfo drive = fileSystem.DriveInfo.New("//build-server"); await That(drive.IsReady).IsTrue(); UNC drives don't appear in DriveInfo.GetDrives(): they're addressable but not enumerated, matching the real behavior.

fileSystem.DriveInfo.GetDrives() returns the registered drives. The objects are full IDriveInfo instances and report TotalSize, AvailableFreeSpace, DriveFormat, VolumeLabel and so on. fileSystem.GetDefaultDrive() returns the drive backing the current working directory, which is convenient when you need to assert against the same drive MockFileSystem is using by default.

The callback passed to WithDrive(...) receives an IStorageDrive whose setters keep working after the test has started, so you can flip a drive offline mid-test or change its format/type without recreating the file system: Setter What it changes SetTotalSize(long) Total disk capacity (defaults to 1 GB) SetDriveFormat(string) The reported DriveFormat (e.g. "NTFS", "ext4") SetDriveType(DriveType) The reported DriveType (Fixed, Removable, Network, …) SetIsReady(bool) Whether the drive reports itself as ready; simulates a removable drive ejecting ChangeUsedBytes(long delta) Mark space as used (or free) without writing files. Throws IOException if free space goes negative MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.WithDrive("E:", d => d.SetDriveType(DriveType.Removable)); // later in the test: simulate the user yanking the USB stick IDriveInfo e = fileSystem.DriveInfo.New("E:"); ((IStorageDrive)e).SetIsReady(false);

IFileSystemExtensibility is the hook that custom strategies (ACL, Unix file mode) use to attach extra data to the mock without bloating the public IFileSystem surface. note You only need IFileSystemExtensibility when you write a custom strategy or extension method. Day-to-day test code never touches it. public interface IFileSystemExtensibility { T? RetrieveMetadata<T>(string key); void StoreMetadata<T>(string key, T? value); bool TryGetWrappedInstance<T>(out T? wrappedInstance); } Any IFileSystemInfo (or FileSystemStream) on the mock can be cast to IFileSystemExtensibility to: Store arbitrary metadata keyed by a string. Survives for the lifetime of the file/directory entry. Retrieve it back later in a strategy callback or another part of the test. Unwrap the underlying real instance when the abstraction happens to point at the real file system. TryGetWrappedInstance<FileInfo>(out FileInfo? fileInfo) returns true and the actual System.IO.FileInfo only on RealFileSystem. A typical pattern in a strategy: public override bool IsAccessGranted(string fullPath, IFileSystemExtensibility extensibility, UnixFileMode mode, AccessRequest request) { string? owner = extensibility.RetrieveMetadata<string>("owner"); return CheckPermissions(mode, owner, request.Access); } public override void OnSetUnixFileMode(string fullPath, IFileSystemExtensibility extensibility, UnixFileMode mode) { extensibility.StoreMetadata("mode", mode); extensibility.StoreMetadata("owner", CurrentUser); }

MockFileSystem ships a fully functional FileSystemWatcher replacement. It fires the same events as the real one and, crucially, it fires the OS-specific events that the real watcher fires on Linux, Windows and macOS.

MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.Initialize().WithSubdirectory("vault"); fileSystem.File.WriteAllBytes("vault/red-square.png", []); using IFileSystemWatcher watcher = fileSystem.FileSystemWatcher.New("vault"); ManualResetEventSlim artworkRemoved = new(); watcher.Deleted += (_, _) => artworkRemoved.Set(); watcher.EnableRaisingEvents = true; fileSystem.File.Delete("vault/red-square.png"); await That(artworkRemoved.Wait(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1))).IsTrue();

MockFileSystem.Watcher.OnTriggered(...) returns an awaitable callback that fires after every IFileSystemWatcher event. Use it to assert what a watcher saw without subscribing to the event yourself: MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.Initialize().WithSubdirectory("vault"); using IFileSystemWatcher watcher = fileSystem.FileSystemWatcher.New("vault"); watcher.EnableRaisingEvents = true; using IAwaitableCallback<WatcherChangeDescription> triggered = fileSystem.Watcher.OnTriggered(); fileSystem.File.WriteAllBytes("vault/blue-circles.png", []); WatcherChangeDescription[] events = triggered.Wait(count: 1);

fileSystem.FileVersionInfo.GetVersionInfo(path) mirrors System.Diagnostics.FileVersionInfo.GetVersionInfo. On the mock, the returned IFileVersionInfo has every field set to null/false by default, since the in-memory file has no PE header. To make a version-info-driven test deterministic, register a builder against a glob pattern with MockFileSystem.WithFileVersionInfo(...): MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.WithFileVersionInfo("*.dll", v => v .SetCompanyName("Abstract Arts") .SetProductName("Gallery Kiosk") .SetProductVersion("1.2.3.4") .SetFileVersion("1.2.3.0") .SetIsDebug(false)); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("Gallery.Kiosk.dll", ""); IFileVersionInfo info = fileSystem.FileVersionInfo.GetVersionInfo("Gallery.Kiosk.dll"); await That(info.CompanyName).IsEqualTo("Abstract Arts"); await That(info.ProductVersion).IsEqualTo("1.2.3.4"); The glob pattern is matched against the file path; the first matching registration wins. The builder exposes a setter for every field on IFileVersionInfo: Comments, CompanyName, FileDescription, FileVersion, InternalName, IsDebug, IsPatched, IsPreRelease, IsPrivateBuild, IsSpecialBuild, Language, LegalCopyright, LegalTrademarks, OriginalFilename, PrivateBuild, ProductName, ProductVersion, SpecialBuild.
You can seed a MockFileSystem declaratively (with descriptions), fluently (with a builder), or by copying data in from outside the test.

Both styles below create: a directory artworks/ containing a sub-directory sketches/ and an empty file red-square.png a file about.txt with content "Welcome to the gallery" Declarative Fluent MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.Initialize().With( new DirectoryDescription("artworks", new DirectoryDescription("sketches"), new FileDescription("red-square.png")), new FileDescription("about.txt", "Welcome to the gallery")); FileDescription also accepts binary content and can mark a file read-only: MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.Initialize().With( new FileDescription("blue-circles.png", new byte[] { 0x89, 0x50, 0x4E, 0x47 }), new FileDescription("catalog.json", "[]") { IsReadOnly = true }); MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.Initialize() .WithSubdirectory("artworks").Initialized(d => d .WithSubdirectory("sketches") .WithFile("red-square.png")) .WithFile("about.txt").Which(f => f.HasStringContent("Welcome to the gallery")); Use HasStringContent(string) or HasBytesContent(byte[]) on the file manipulator to set content.

fileSystem.InitializeIn("gallery") .WithASubdirectory() .WithSubdirectory("artworks").Initialized(s => s .WithAFile()) .WithFile("about.txt"); This sets gallery as the working directory and seeds it with: a randomly named sub-directory an artworks/ sub-directory containing one randomly named file an about.txt file WithASubdirectory() / WithAFile() use generated names when you don't care about the exact value, which is useful for tests that operate over whatever they find. WithAFile(string extension) lets you constrain the random name to a specific extension. InitializeIn(absolutePath) automatically registers the corresponding drive on Windows when the path is rooted.
fileSystem.Initialize() .WithSubdirectories("artworks/sketches/2026", "vault/restricted", "exports"); Creates each path (and any missing parents) in one call.

Initialize() returns an IFileSystemInitializer<TFileSystem> exposing: BaseDirectory: the IDirectoryInfo of the seed root FileSystem: the underlying file system this[int index]: the created entries in the order they were added IFileSystemInitializer<MockFileSystem> init = fileSystem.Initialize() .WithFile("catalog.json") .WithSubdirectory("artworks"); IFileInfo catalog = (IFileInfo)init[0]; IDirectoryInfo artworks = (IDirectoryInfo)init[1];

fileSystem.InitializeFromRealDirectory("test-data"); // or copy the source directory into a different target on the mock: fileSystem.InitializeFromRealDirectory(@"C:\fixtures\sample-collection", "collection"); Recursively copies every file and sub-directory from the real path into the mock, preserving creation/last-write/last-access time and attributes. With large fixtures this can be slow, so prefer it for small, hand-curated test data.

fileSystem.InitializeEmbeddedResourcesFromAssembly( directoryPath: "fixtures", assembly: typeof(GalleryTests).Assembly, relativePath: "TestData", searchPattern: "*.json", searchOption: SearchOption.AllDirectories); Materializes embedded resources as files inside the mock. Resource names are split on the last . to recover an extension (e.g. GalleryTests.TestData.artworks.json becomes fixtures/artworks.json). relativePath filters which resources are included; searchPattern and searchOption work like Directory.EnumerateFiles.

By default, Initialize() and InitializeIn() also materialize the system temp directory inside the mock, so code that calls Path.GetTempPath() finds something there. Pass an options callback to opt out: fileSystem.Initialize(o => o.InitializeTempDirectory = false);

The fluent builders throw TestingException (in Testably.Abstractions.Testing.Initializer) when used incorrectly, for example when calling WithFile("catalog.json") twice in the same parent scope. Catch this type if you need to surface a friendly assertion in a custom helper.

For integration tests that hit the real disk, SetCurrentDirectoryToEmptyTemporaryDirectory creates a fresh temp directory, switches Directory.GetCurrentDirectory() to it, and force-deletes everything when the returned IDirectoryCleaner is disposed: IFileSystem fileSystem = new RealFileSystem(); using IDirectoryCleaner cleaner = fileSystem.SetCurrentDirectoryToEmptyTemporaryDirectory(prefix: "GalleryTests-"); // fileSystem.Directory.GetCurrentDirectory() is now an empty temp directory // On dispose: the directory is force-deleted (read-only flag and all) The prefix parameter makes leftovers easier to spot in %TEMP% if cleanup ever fails. The optional logger parameter receives diagnostic messages (e.g. retry attempts when antivirus holds a file open). If you need a temporary directory but want to leave Directory.GetCurrentDirectory() untouched, use CreateEmptyTemporaryDirectory instead. It behaves identically (same prefix and logger parameters, same force-delete on dispose) but does not change the current directory: IFileSystem fileSystem = new RealFileSystem(); using IDirectoryCleaner cleaner = fileSystem.CreateEmptyTemporaryDirectory(prefix: "GalleryTests-"); // fileSystem.Directory.GetCurrentDirectory() is unchanged // Use cleaner.BasePath to access the empty temp directory // On dispose: the directory is force-deleted (read-only flag and all)

documents.t: MockFileSystem exposes three hooks for reacting to file system activity in tests: Intercept runs before an operation completes and can throw to abort it. Notify runs after an operation completes and supports awaiting the next event. Watcher runs after the IFileSystemWatcher raised an event; see FileSystemWatcher. All three return an IAwaitableCallback<T> (with T being ChangeDescription for Intercept and Notify, and WatcherChangeDescription for Watcher): Dispose() removes the subscription. Wait(int count = 1, TimeSpan? timeout = null) blocks until count events arrived; defaults to a 30-second timeout. WaitAsync(...) is the async counterpart and additionally accepts a CancellationToken. The time system's notifications use the same IAwaitableCallback<T>.

MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.Intercept.Creating(FileSystemTypes.File, _ => throw new IOException("The vault is full."), globPattern: "*.png"); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("catalog.json", "[]"); // ok fileSystem.File.WriteAllBytes("red-square.png", []); // throws "The vault is full." Useful for simulating disk errors, permission failures or race conditions. IInterceptionHandler exposes Changing, Creating and Deleting extensions. Each takes a FileSystemTypes (File, Directory or DirectoryOrFile), an optional globPattern (defaults to "*") and an optional predicate for finer filtering.

The examples below use the CatalogService from Getting started, which writes exports/catalog.json. MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); using IAwaitableCallback<ChangeDescription> notify = fileSystem.Notify .OnCreated(FileSystemTypes.File); new CatalogService(fileSystem).Export("[]"); ChangeDescription[] events = notify.Wait(count: 1); await That(events[0].Path).EndsWith("catalog.json"); tip Register the callback first, then do the work, then call Wait (or WaitAsync in an async test). This is deterministic, unlike polling with Task.Delay. OnChanged, OnCreated and OnDeleted are all available, with the same globPattern / predicate filters as Intercept.

OnEventOrReplay works like OnEvent, but also replays the matching changes that happened before the subscription, in their original order. That helps when the work is already done by the time the test can subscribe: MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); new CatalogService(fileSystem).Export("[]"); using IAwaitableCallback<ChangeDescription> notify = fileSystem.Notify.OnEventOrReplay( predicate: c => c.ChangeType == WatcherChangeTypes.Created && c.FileSystemType == FileSystemTypes.File); ChangeDescription[] events = notify.Wait(count: 1); await That(events[0].Path).EndsWith("catalog.json"); fileSystem.Watcher.OnTriggeredOrReplay(...) does the same for watcher events. The history is recorded by default; new MockFileSystem(o => o.WithoutNotificationHistory()) turns it off, and both methods then throw InvalidOperationException.

.NET 6 or later ToAsyncEnumerable is only available on .NET 6 and later. You can stream the same callback as an async sequence: await foreach (ChangeDescription change in fileSystem.Notify.OnCreated(FileSystemTypes.File).ToAsyncEnumerable()) { // process every file creation as it happens } The sequence ends without an exception after 30 seconds, so the loop cannot hang forever. Pass an explicit timeout (TimeSpan? or int milliseconds) or a CancellationToken to end it earlier or later.

IFileSystem.RandomAccess abstracts the static methods on System.IO.RandomAccess. It reads and writes a file through a SafeFileHandle at an explicit offset, without a stream in between. Every method is positionless: the offset is a parameter, not state carried on the handle. Nothing advances, so two reads at the same offset return the same bytes and concurrent writes at different offsets do not interfere. MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.File.WriteAllBytes("red-square.png", [1, 2, 3, 4]); using SafeFileHandle handle = fileSystem.File.OpenHandle("red-square.png", FileMode.Open, FileAccess.ReadWrite); byte[] buffer = new byte[2]; fileSystem.RandomAccess.Read(handle, buffer, fileOffset: 1); // buffer is [2, 3] fileSystem.RandomAccess.Write(handle, new byte[] { 9 }, fileOffset: 0); await That(fileSystem.File.ReadAllBytes("red-square.png")) .IsEqualTo(new byte[] { 9, 2, 3, 4 }); Get the handle from IFile.OpenHandle, so the file system it came from can resolve it.

Member Available from GetLength .NET 6 Read, ReadAsync .NET 6 Write, WriteAsync .NET 6 SetLength .NET 8 FlushToDisk .NET 8 Read and Write each have a scatter/gather overload taking an IReadOnlyList<Memory<byte>>, which fills or consumes the buffers in order as though they were one.

A read whose offset is at or past the end of the file returns 0; a read that runs off the end returns a short count rather than throwing. A write past the end grows the file and zero-fills the gap. SetLength truncates, or grows with zeroes. GetLength is metadata and works on a write-only handle. Reading a write-only handle, or writing a read-only one, throws UnauthorizedAccessException. On a handle opened with FileMode.Append the offset is still honored: RandomAccess does not append for you. Operations on a disposed handle throw ObjectDisposedException.

FlushToDisk asks the operating system to make prior writes durable. The MockFileSystem keeps its files in memory and has no write-back cache, so there is nothing to flush, but the call is still resolved against the handle and recorded, so a test can assert that a durability barrier was requested: MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("guard-rounds.log", null); using (SafeFileHandle handle = fileSystem.File.OpenHandle("guard-rounds.log", FileMode.Open, FileAccess.Write)) { fileSystem.RandomAccess.Write(handle, "round"u8.ToArray(), 0); fileSystem.RandomAccess.FlushToDisk(handle); } await That(fileSystem.Statistics.RandomAccess.Methods) .Contains(m => m.Name == nameof(IRandomAccess.FlushToDisk)); That is something the real file system cannot tell you, and it is the reason to reach for the abstraction rather than the static class: code that needs a durability barrier can be tested for asking.
SafeFileHandle is a wrapper around an OS handle to a real file, and overloads like File.GetLastAccessTime(SafeFileHandle) route through it.

IFile.OpenHandle returns a handle that the file system it came from understands, so nothing has to be registered: MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("red-square.txt", "Oil on board"); using SafeFileHandle handle = fileSystem.File.OpenHandle("red-square.txt"); await That(fileSystem.File.GetLastAccessTime(handle)) .IsEqualTo(fileSystem.File.GetLastAccessTime("red-square.txt")); await That(fileSystem.RandomAccess.GetLength(handle)).IsEqualTo(12); Like a real handle, it refers to the file it was opened on rather than to its name, so it keeps working after the file is renamed. It also honors the FileShare and FileOptions (including DeleteOnClose) it was opened with, following the rules of the simulated operating system. Only for the abstraction A handle the MockFileSystem created is not a real OS handle, so passing it to System.IO.RandomAccess or to another process fails. Use IFileSystem.RandomAccess and the IFile overloads instead. note The mock cannot observe the moment a handle is disposed, so a released share lock or DeleteOnClose takes effect the next time the file system checks whether the file exists or may be opened.

When a handle comes from somewhere the mock knows nothing about (platform invocation, or a library that hands you one), you still have to tell it which file that handle stands for. MockFileSystem.WithSafeFileHandleStrategy(SafeFileHandleStrategy) registers the translation. The strategy maps a SafeFileHandle to a SafeFileHandleMock that points at a location inside the mock, and is consulted for any handle the mock did not create itself. The default strategy (NullSafeFileHandleStrategy) is registered automatically and throws NotSupportedException for any handle. Install a custom strategy as soon as your code under test reaches for a handle from outside.

The strategy below keeps an explicit map from SafeFileHandle to (real path, mock path). On every lookup it copies the real file's attributes and timestamps into the mock, so the test sees fresh data without having to write a fixture by hand. CustomSafeFileHandleStrategy public class CustomSafeFileHandleStrategy : SafeFileHandleStrategy { private readonly RealFileSystem _realFileSystem; private readonly MockFileSystem _mockFileSystem; private readonly Dictionary<SafeFileHandle, (string RealPath, SafeFileHandleMock Mock)> _mapping = new(); public CustomSafeFileHandleStrategy( RealFileSystem realFileSystem, MockFileSystem mockFileSystem) { _realFileSystem = realFileSystem; _mockFileSystem = mockFileSystem; } public CustomSafeFileHandleStrategy AddMapping( SafeFileHandle handle, string realPath, SafeFileHandleMock mock) { _mapping[handle] = (realPath, mock); return this; } public override SafeFileHandleMock MapSafeFileHandle(SafeFileHandle handle) { if (!_mapping.TryGetValue(handle, out (string RealPath, SafeFileHandleMock Mock) entry)) throw new KeyNotFoundException("The provided fileHandle is not mapped!"); SyncMetadata(entry.RealPath, entry.Mock.Path); return entry.Mock; } private void SyncMetadata(string realPath, string mockPath) { _mockFileSystem.File.SetAttributes(mockPath, _realFileSystem.File.GetAttributes(realPath)); _mockFileSystem.File.SetCreationTime(mockPath, _realFileSystem.File.GetCreationTime(realPath)); _mockFileSystem.File.SetLastAccessTime(mockPath, _realFileSystem.File.GetLastAccessTime(realPath)); _mockFileSystem.File.SetLastWriteTime(mockPath, _realFileSystem.File.GetLastWriteTime(realPath)); } }

documents.t: RealFileSystem realFileSystem = new(); MockFileSystem mockFileSystem = new(); CustomSafeFileHandleStrategy strategy = new(realFileSystem, mockFileSystem); mockFileSystem.WithSafeFileHandleStrategy(strategy); using IDirectoryCleaner _ = realFileSystem.SetCurrentDirectoryToEmptyTemporaryDirectory(); // Create the same file on both sides mockFileSystem.File.WriteAllText("mock", "Oil on board"); realFileSystem.File.WriteAllText("real", "Oil on board"); // Mutate the real file's last-access time DateTime expected = new DateTime(2026, 1, 1); realFileSystem.File.SetLastAccessTime("real", expected); // Open a SafeFileHandle on the real file SafeFileHandle handle = realFileSystem.File.OpenHandle("real"); // Register the mapping strategy.AddMapping(handle, "real", new SafeFileHandleMock("mock")); // Reading via the SafeFileHandle goes through the strategy and synchronizes // the mock metadata from the real file system on the way in await That(mockFileSystem.File.GetLastAccessTime(handle)).IsEqualTo(expected); // As a side effect the mock path now also reflects the synced value await That(mockFileSystem.File.GetLastAccessTime("mock")).IsEqualTo(expected); Here the handle belongs to the real file system, so the mock cannot resolve it on its own and the strategy supplies the mapping. A handle from mockFileSystem.File.OpenHandle needs none of this.

MockFileSystem can pretend to be a different operating system than the host it runs on. Pass a SimulationMode in the constructor: Linux Windows macOS MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(o => o.SimulatingOperatingSystem(SimulationMode.Linux)); // case-sensitive, '/' separator, single root MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(o => o.SimulatingOperatingSystem(SimulationMode.Windows)); // case-insensitive, '\' separator, drive letters MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(o => o.SimulatingOperatingSystem(SimulationMode.MacOS)); // case-insensitive, '/' separator, single root Because the entire test suite runs against the real file system on Linux, macOS and Windows and against each SimulationMode in CI, the simulated behavior stays in lock-step with the genuine platform behavior over time. .NET 6 or later SimulatingOperatingSystem is only available on .NET 6 and later. On older targets, the mock always uses the host OS.

Catch case-sensitivity bugs that only show up on Linux from a Windows dev machine. Verify path-handling code on Windows from a Linux CI runner. Test drive-letter handling without spinning up a Windows job. If you only need the host's own behavior, omit SimulatingOperatingSystem: MockFileSystem defaults to whichever OS it is running on.

MockFileSystem.Statistics records every call made through the mock: which property was accessed, which method was invoked, with what arguments. Use it to assert what a system under test did, not just what it produced. MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("catalog.json", "[]"); fileSystem.File.ReadAllText("catalog.json"); IFileSystemStatistics stats = fileSystem.Statistics; await That(stats.TotalCount).IsEqualTo(2); await That(stats.File.Methods).Contains(m => m.Name == nameof(IFile.WriteAllText));

IFileSystemStatistics exposes one property per IFileSystem sub-property (Directory, DirectoryInfo, DriveInfo, File, FileInfo, FileStream, FileSystemWatcher, FileVersionInfo, Path and RandomAccess). Each of them has Methods and Properties collections. An entry carries the call's name, its parameters and a global Counter that tells the order of the calls. The properties for types created by a factory (DirectoryInfo, DriveInfo, FileInfo, FileStream, FileSystemWatcher, FileVersionInfo) also have an indexer keyed by path: stats.FileInfo["catalog.json"] returns just the calls made on the IFileInfo for that path: _ = fileSystem.FileInfo.New("catalog.json").Exists; await That(stats.FileInfo["catalog.json"].Properties) .Contains(p => p.Name == nameof(IFileInfo.Exists)); TotalCount returns the sum across every sub-property, which is handy for "did anything touch the file system at all?" assertions.

Calls inside the testing helpers themselves (Initialize, InitializeFromRealDirectory, SetCurrentDirectoryToEmptyTemporaryDirectory, …) are excluded from the statistics so seeding does not pollute your assertions.

To simulate POSIX permissions in the mock, derive from the abstract UnixFileModeStrategy base class and plug it in via WithUnixFileModeStrategy(...). Without one, the mock grants access to every entry whose UnixFileMode is not None. The strategy decides: whether a given user/group is allowed to read or write a path (IsAccessGranted); the AccessRequest contains the requested FileAccess, and deleting a file or directory is not checked what to record when the file mode is set, for example by File.SetUnixFileMode(...) (optionally override OnSetUnixFileMode, which does nothing by default) A typical implementation stores the file's user and group alongside the file via IFileSystemExtensibility, then uses that data plus the file's UnixFileMode to decide whether to grant access. When access is denied, the mock throws UnauthorizedAccessException. Not on Windows WithUnixFileModeStrategy throws PlatformNotSupportedException when the host (or simulated OS) is Windows. On a Windows machine, simulate Linux or macOS.

The strategy below is not part of the library; copy and adapt it. It lets a test simulate "running as user X in group Y" via fluent setters and records the simulated user and group as the owner whenever the mode of an entry is set. It grants read access when: the mode includes OtherRead, or the mode includes GroupRead and the owner's group matches the simulated group, or the mode includes UserRead and the owner matches the simulated user The same rules apply to write access with the *Write flags. SimulatedUserStrategy public class SimulatedUserStrategy : UnixFileModeStrategy { private string _user = ""; private string _group = ""; public SimulatedUserStrategy SimulateUser(string user) { _user = user; return this; } public SimulatedUserStrategy SimulateGroup(string group) { _group = group; return this; } public override void OnSetUnixFileMode(string fullPath, IFileSystemExtensibility extensibility, UnixFileMode mode) { // Record the simulated owner at the moment the file's mode was set extensibility.StoreMetadata(nameof(SimulatedUserStrategy), new UserGroup(_user, _group)); } public override bool IsAccessGranted(string fullPath, IFileSystemExtensibility extensibility, UnixFileMode mode, AccessRequest request) { UserGroup owner = extensibility .RetrieveMetadata<UserGroup>(nameof(SimulatedUserStrategy)) ?? new UserGroup(_user, _group); bool readOk = mode.HasFlag(UnixFileMode.OtherRead) || (mode.HasFlag(UnixFileMode.GroupRead) && owner.Group == _group) || (mode.HasFlag(UnixFileMode.UserRead) && owner.User == _user); bool writeOk = mode.HasFlag(UnixFileMode.OtherWrite) || (mode.HasFlag(UnixFileMode.GroupWrite) && owner.Group == _group) || (mode.HasFlag(UnixFileMode.UserWrite) && owner.User == _user); return request.Access switch { FileAccess.Read => readOk, FileAccess.Write => writeOk, _ => readOk && writeOk, }; } private record UserGroup(string User, string Group); }

SimulatedUserStrategy strategy = new(); MockFileSystem fileSystem = new MockFileSystem(o => o .SimulatingOperatingSystem(SimulationMode.Linux)) .WithUnixFileModeStrategy(strategy); // "alice" creates a directory readable only by the group "curators" strategy.SimulateUser("alice").SimulateGroup("curators"); fileSystem.Directory.CreateDirectory("restoration", UnixFileMode.GroupRead); // "bob" (also a curator) can read it strategy.SimulateUser("bob").SimulateGroup("curators"); fileSystem.Directory.GetFiles("restoration"); // no exception // switch to a different group → read denied strategy.SimulateGroup("visitors"); fileSystem.Directory.GetFiles("restoration"); // throws UnauthorizedAccessException

strategy.SimulateUser("alice"); fileSystem.Directory.CreateDirectory("vault", UnixFileMode.UserWrite); strategy.SimulateUser("bob"); Action act = () => fileSystem.Directory.CreateDirectory("vault/drafts"); await That(act).Throws<UnauthorizedAccessException>();

.NET Standard 2.0 or later The packages target .NET Standard 2.0 and 2.1, .NET 6, .NET 8, .NET 9, .NET 10 and .NET 11, so they also work in .NET Framework projects. Some members are only available on newer target frameworks; the pages that describe them say so.

Install Testably.Abstractions in your production projects: .NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package Testably.Abstractions <PackageReference Include="Testably.Abstractions" Version="10.4.0" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="Testably.Abstractions" Version="10.4.0" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="Testably.Abstractions" /> Latest version: 10.4.0 and Testably.Abstractions.Testing in your test projects: .NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package Testably.Abstractions.Testing <PackageReference Include="Testably.Abstractions.Testing" Version="7.2.0" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="Testably.Abstractions.Testing" Version="7.2.0" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="Testably.Abstractions.Testing" /> Latest version: 7.2.0 Package Install it in Testably.Abstractions Production code: contains RealFileSystem, RealTimeSystem and RealRandomSystem Testably.Abstractions.Testing Test projects: contains MockFileSystem, MockTimeSystem and MockRandomSystem Testably.Abstractions.Interface Libraries that only consume IFileSystem, ITimeSystem or IRandomSystem and leave the choice of implementation to the application Testably.Abstractions.FileSystem.Interface Libraries that only need IFileSystem Both Testably.Abstractions and Testably.Abstractions.Testing pull in the interface packages transitively. Optional companion packages add compression, access control and memory-mapped files; each page shows how to install it.

With Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection: Program.cs builder.Services .AddSingleton<IFileSystem, RealFileSystem>() .AddSingleton<IRandomSystem, RealRandomSystem>() .AddSingleton<ITimeSystem, RealTimeSystem>();

CatalogService.cs public class CatalogService(IFileSystem fileSystem) { public void Export(string json) { fileSystem.Directory.CreateDirectory("exports"); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("exports/catalog.json", json); } }
documents.s: Use the interfaces in your services

documents.t: In the test, replace the real implementation with the mock: CatalogServiceTests.cs using Testably.Abstractions.Testing; using static aweXpect.Expect; public class CatalogServiceTests { [Test] public async Task Export_ShouldWriteCatalogToExportsFolder() { MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); CatalogService sut = new(fileSystem); sut.Export("""{ "title": "Red Square" }"""); await That(fileSystem.File.ReadAllText("exports/catalog.json")) .IsEqualTo("""{ "title": "Red Square" }"""); } } That's it: your code now runs against an in-memory file system in tests, and against the real one in production. About the examples The examples in this documentation are set in a gallery of abstract art: a catalog of artworks, exhibitions that open and close, and a night guard on patrol. They use TUnit and check results with aweXpect. Neither is required: the mocks work with any test framework and assertion library.

A complete example: one gallery service tested with the file system, time and random system together. File system: IFileSystem, MockFileSystem, drives, watcher, statistics, strategies. Time system: ITimeSystem, time providers, timers, auto-advance, notifications. Random system: IRandomSystem and deterministic generators. Companion libraries: Compression, AccessControl and MemoryMappedFiles. aweXpect.Testably: expectations for the file system and time system mocks, if you use aweXpect.
Testably.Abstractions and TestableIO.System.IO.Abstractions share the same IFileSystem interface, so production code does not need to change when you switch testing libraries.

The shared IFileSystem interface means production code is identical either way; this choice only affects tests. The core differentiator: Testably.Abstractions runs its full test suite against both MockFileSystem and RealFileSystem on every supported OS and against each SimulationMode, so the mock and the real OS stay in lock-step over time. Pick Testably.Abstractions when you need a watcher, SafeFileHandle, multiple drives with size quotas, the ITimeSystem / IRandomSystem companions, or you want to exercise Linux/macOS/Windows behavior from a single CI job. Pick TestableIO.System.IO.Abstractions when you're already using its MockFileData / MockDirectoryData to inspect or mutate the in-memory store directly; that surface has no equivalent here.
The migration only affects your test projects. There are two paths; pick one.

The Testably.Abstractions.Migration analyzer rewrites the supported call sites for you. Install it alongside Testably.Abstractions.Testing, apply the code fix from your IDE or dotnet format analyzers, then uninstall it. Patterns it cannot rewrite safely are still reported so you can address them by hand; see the analyzer page for the full mapping table and recommended workflow.

If you'd rather not introduce a build-time analyzer, swap the package and rewrite the call sites yourself. Swap the package: <!-- Remove --> <PackageReference Include="TestableIO.System.IO.Abstractions.TestingHelpers" /> <!-- Add --> <PackageReference Include="Testably.Abstractions.Testing" /> Update the test code: // Before (TestableIO) MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.AddDirectory("artworks"); fileSystem.AddFile("artworks/red-square.txt", new MockFileData("Oil on canvas")); // After (Testably), option A: imperative MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.Directory.CreateDirectory("artworks"); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("artworks/red-square.txt", "Oil on canvas"); // After (Testably), option B: fluent initialization MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.Initialize() .WithSubdirectory("artworks").Initialized(d => d .WithFile("red-square.txt").Which(f => f .HasStringContent("Oil on canvas"))); Production code keeps using IFileSystem exactly as before; no changes there.

Testably.Abstractions.Migration is a Roslyn analyzer that automates the call-site rewrites from TestableIO to Testably.Abstractions described on the migration overview. It flags every supported pattern (with code-fix support) and reports the rest so you can address them by hand.

The migration package is a one-shot development tool: install it, migrate, then uninstall. It ships only the analyzer and code fixer, no runtime code, and is marked as a DevelopmentDependency so it never flows transitively to consumers of your test project. Because the package does not pull Testably.Abstractions.Testing transitively, you must reference it yourself in the project being migrated. Otherwise the rewritten call sites would compile while the migration package is installed but stop compiling the moment you remove it. .NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package Testably.Abstractions.Testing <PackageReference Include="Testably.Abstractions.Testing" Version="7.2.0" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="Testably.Abstractions.Testing" Version="7.2.0" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="Testably.Abstractions.Testing" /> Latest version: 7.2.0 Then add the migration package: .NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package Testably.Abstractions.Migration <PackageReference Include="Testably.Abstractions.Migration" Version="0.2.0" PrivateAssets="all" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="Testably.Abstractions.Migration" Version="0.2.0" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="Testably.Abstractions.Migration" PrivateAssets="all" /> Latest version: 0.2.0

Reference the target library. Add Testably.Abstractions.Testing to the project you want to migrate (see above). Existing TestableIO.System.IO.Abstractions.TestingHelpers usage keeps compiling side-by-side. Install the migration package. Adds the analyzer. Every supported construct is reported as warning TestablyM001. Apply the code fix. Use your IDE (Visual Studio, Rider, VS Code with C# Dev Kit) to fix diagnostics one by one, or run dotnet format analyzers to apply every available fix in bulk. Address manual-review diagnostics. Some patterns have no safe automatic rewrite (see Manual review). The analyzer reports them so they are discoverable; you migrate each call site by hand. Remove TestableIO.System.IO.Abstractions.TestingHelpers. Once the analyzer is quiet, drop the dependency (or System.IO.Abstractions.TestingHelpers, the older package id that forwards to it). Uninstall the migration package. It has served its purpose and only adds analyzer overhead from here on. dotnet remove package TestableIO.System.IO.Abstractions.TestingHelpers dotnet remove package Testably.Abstractions.Migration

The analyzer emits a single diagnostic id, TestablyM001. Each call site carries a pattern property in Diagnostic.Properties that tells the code-fix provider which rewrite to perform. Patterns without an automatic rewrite still get a TestablyM001 warning so you can locate them; the code fix just declines to register an action. Reads of MockFileData properties (e.g. fs.GetFile(path).LastWriteTime) are routed to the matching Testably file-system call (e.g. fs.File.GetLastWriteTime(path)). Writes (e.g. fs.GetFile(path).LastWriteTime = value) become fs.File.SetLastWriteTime(path, value). The fixer only handles the one-shot fs.GetFile(path).Prop shape; property access through a captured reference is left for manual review (see below).

These call sites are flagged with TestablyM001 but have no automatic rewrite, either because Testably.Abstractions has no equivalent surface or because a safe rewrite would require flow analysis the analyzer does not perform. Address each one by hand. Pattern Why manual MockFileData.AccessControl Use SetAccessControl from the AccessControl companion package; to deny access, register a strategy with WithAccessControlStrategy. MockFileData.AllowedFileShare Testably honors the FileShare a file was opened with; keep a stream with the restricted share open instead. MockFileData.UnixMode Use File.SetUnixFileMode; to enforce the permissions, register a strategy with WithUnixFileModeStrategy. new MockFileVersionInfo(...) Register the version information for a path pattern with WithFileVersionInfo. Subclassing MockFileSystem / MockFileData Inheritance contract differs in Testably. new MockFileData(MockFileData template) Copy-clone semantics differ; no Testably equivalent. Captured-reference MockFileData property access var data = fs.GetFile(path); data.Prop = … cannot be rewritten without local flow analysis. fs.AllPaths / AllFiles / AllDirectories / AllDrives Testably has no enumeration properties; the natural replacements need a root or drive scope the analyzer cannot infer. fs.MockTime(Func<DateTime>) TestableIO calls the delegate per timestamp request; Testably installs a fixed-then-mutable MockTimeSystem at construction. No observably-equivalent automatic rewrite for arbitrary delegates. fs.AddFileFromEmbeddedResource(...) Testably exposes only a bulk InitializeEmbeddedResourcesFromAssembly with path-style matching; the single-file mapping is not safe to automate.

If you choose not to migrate a particular call site, suppress TestablyM001 per usage with the standard mechanisms: #pragma warning disable TestablyM001 MockFileSystem fs = new MockFileSystem(); #pragma warning restore TestablyM001 or via an .editorconfig entry scoped to the file/folder: .editorconfig [**/Legacy/**.cs] dotnet_diagnostic.TestablyM001.severity = none
IRandomSystem wraps the two non-deterministic primitives most code reaches for: Random and Guid.
Sub-property Wraps Random new Random() and Random.Shared, including a thread-safe shared instance under .NET Framework Guid Guid.NewGuid() and the related factories

Type Package Use it for RealRandomSystem Testably.Abstractions Production MockRandomSystem Testably.Abstractions.Testing Unit tests IRandomSystem randomSystem = new MockRandomSystem(); int n = randomSystem.Random.Shared.Next(100); Guid id = randomSystem.Guid.NewGuid(); By default the mock produces unpredictable values, like the real system, which is useful for catching code that accidentally depends on a specific output. See Deterministic randomness for how to drive Random and Guid from a known sequence.

For snapshot tests, generated-id assertions, or reproducing a reported bug, you want the "random" values to be predictable. RandomProvider.Generate(...) lets you supply a generator for any of the primitive types Random produces: IRandomProvider provider = RandomProvider.Generate( seed: 42, intGenerator: new[] { 1, 2, 3 }, // round-robins through the array guidGenerator: () => Guid.Parse("00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001"), doubleGenerator: 0.5); // always returns 0.5 MockRandomSystem randomSystem = new(provider); randomSystem.Random.Shared.Next(); // 1 randomSystem.Random.Shared.Next(); // 2 randomSystem.Random.Shared.Next(); // 3 randomSystem.Random.Shared.Next(); // 1 (wraps around) randomSystem.Guid.NewGuid(); // 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001 Generate accepts generators for int, long, float, double, byte[] and Guid. Any generator left as null falls through to the seeded Random.

Generator<T> has implicit conversions from T, T[] and Func<T>, plus four explicit factory methods so most call sites stay terse: // From a single value (every call returns 42): implicit, or explicit Generator.FromValue(42) Generator<int> g1 = 42; // From an array (round-robin): implicit, or explicit Generator.FromArray(new[] { 1, 2, 3 }) Generator<int> g2 = new[] { 1, 2, 3 }; // From a callback: implicit from Func<T>, or explicit Generator.FromCallback(...) Generator<int> g3 = Generator.FromCallback(() => DateTime.Now.Millisecond); // From any IEnumerable (loops once exhausted) Generator<Guid> g4 = Generator.FromEnumerable(catalogNumbers); If you have a Generator<T> directly, g.GetNext() returns the next value, which is useful when you build the generator yourself outside a MockRandomSystem (e.g. for parameterized test-data generation). Generator<T> is IDisposable: when wrapping an IEnumerable<T>, dispose it (or rely on garbage collection in tests) to release the underlying enumerator.

MockFileSystem uses the random system internally for things like Path.GetRandomFileName() and WithAFile(). Pass a deterministic provider through to keep file-system tests reproducible: MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(o => o.UseRandomProvider(RandomProvider.Generate(seed: 1234)));

documents.t: ITimeSystem wraps everything in the BCL that depends on the wall clock or makes a thread wait. Replace it with a MockTimeSystem in tests and you can fast-forward time without sleeping.
