By default, MockTimeSystem advances its clock every time the code under test waits. A call to Thread.Sleep(5s) or Task.Delay(5s) returns immediately and the next read of DateTime.Now reflects 5 seconds later. This is the right default: most tests want to skip the wait, not enforce it. MockTimeSystem timeSystem = new(new DateTime(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc)); await timeSystem.Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10)); await That(timeSystem.DateTime.UtcNow) .IsEqualTo(new DateTime(2026, 1, 1, 0, 10, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc));

A timer moves the clock to its due time as well. The timers that are due on the way fire in the order of their due time, and each callback sees the clock at its own due time, not at the end of the wait. Like a real timer, a callback runs on another thread with the execution context of the code that created the timer, while the thread that moves the clock waits until it completes. When the callback waits for the clock, i.e. for Task.Delay, PeriodicTimer.WaitForNextTickAsync or ITimerMock.Wait of the MockTimeSystem, the clock moves on at once, just like the real clock keeps running. When it blocks on anything else, e.g. on another timer through an event or on a lock that the waiting code holds, the clock moves on once it was blocked for one second of real time. A callback that keeps running, e.g. on a busy machine, holds the clock for up to 30 seconds. All timers move the clock on one shared background thread. Another thread that moves the clock at the same time, e.g. a Task.Delay or AdvanceBy in the test, can move it further while a callback runs. A timer without a period whose state is a CancellationTokenSource is a timeout. This includes the timer of new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan, TimeProvider) on the TimeProvider from ToTimeProvider(), a Timer.New that cancels the CancellationTokenSource it gets as state, and the timer of Task.WaitAsync(TimeSpan, TimeProvider). A timeout never moves the clock on its own: it fires when a wait or AdvanceBy moves the clock past its due time, so that an operation with a timeout is not canceled before it starts. A one-shot timer that does other work should therefore not get a CancellationTokenSource as state. MockTimeSystem timeSystem = new(); TimeProvider timeProvider = timeSystem.ToTimeProvider(); using CancellationTokenSource cts = new(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), timeProvider); // Throws an OperationCanceledException, with the clock one second later await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5), timeProvider, cts.Token); A wait that its timeout cancels on the way stops the clock at the timeout. This applies to Task.Delay and PeriodicTimer.WaitForNextTickAsync of the MockTimeSystem and to Task.Delay on the TimeProvider. Waiting only for a timeout As a timeout never moves the clock, code that waits for nothing but a timeout, e.g. Task.Delay(Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan, timeProvider, cts.Token), waits until something else moves the clock. Only Task.Delay(Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan) of the MockTimeSystem itself returns immediately with auto-advance.

When you need to assert that code waited (instead of just letting it through), turn auto-advance off via MockTimeSystemOptions.DisableAutoAdvance() and move the clock yourself with TimeProvider.AdvanceBy(...) or TimeProvider.SetTo(...): MockTimeSystem timeSystem = new(o => o.DisableAutoAdvance()); Task delay = timeSystem.Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10)); await That(delay.IsCompleted).IsFalse(); timeSystem.TimeProvider.AdvanceBy(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10)); await delay; // completes, because the clock has reached the end of the delay With auto-advance off: Call Behavior Task.Delay Stays pending until the clock reaches the end of the delay PeriodicTimer.WaitForNextTickAsync Stays pending until the clock reaches the next tick Thread.Sleep Returns immediately without moving the clock Timer Fires when AdvanceBy reaches its due time; AdvanceBy waits for it Awaiting a delay with auto-advance off Awaiting Task.Delay before anything advances the clock waits forever. Start the delay, advance the clock (or let another task do it), then await it. Combine this with the notifications hooks to assert what your code asked for.

All threads share one simulated clock, so two parallel Sleep(5s) calls move it by 10 seconds total, which can be surprising. If your test exercises real parallelism, swap in the thread-aware provider so each async context has its own clock.

MockTimeSystem gets its current time from an ITimeProvider. Three factories cover most cases: // 1. Random instant per test (default, useful for catching tests that pass only "today") new MockTimeSystem(); // 2. Pin to a specific instant (UTC if Kind is Unspecified) new MockTimeSystem(new DateTime(2026, 1, 15, 10, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc)); // 3. Use the host's current wall clock new MockTimeSystem(TimeProviderFactory.Now()); TimeProviderFactory.Use(DateTime), TimeProviderFactory.Random() and TimeProviderFactory.Now() all return an ITimeProviderFactory you can pass to the MockTimeSystem constructor.

MockTimeSystem exposes a controllable local time zone through timeSystem.TimeZoneInfo (an ITimeZoneInfo), and uses it to convert the simulated instant for DateTime.Now, DateTime.Today and DateTimeOffset.Now. This makes time-zone-dependent code deterministic instead of depending on the machine the test runs on. The factory picks the initial local time zone: // The parameterless constructor, Now() and Use(DateTime) default the local // time zone to the host's TimeZoneInfo.Local new MockTimeSystem(); new MockTimeSystem(TimeProviderFactory.Now()); // TimeProviderFactory.Random() also picks a random local time zone from a curated, // cross-platform set (including one with daylight-saving-time transitions) new MockTimeSystem(TimeProviderFactory.Random()); // Pin both the instant and the local time zone TimeZoneInfo tokyo = TimeZoneInfo.CreateCustomTimeZone( "Test/Tokyo", TimeSpan.FromHours(9), "Test JST", "Test JST"); new MockTimeSystem(TimeProviderFactory.Use( new DateTime(2026, 1, 15, 0, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc), tokyo)); Change it at runtime (and register additional zones for FindSystemTimeZoneById / GetSystemTimeZones) through the time provider: MockTimeSystem timeSystem = new( new DateTime(2026, 1, 15, 0, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc)); TimeZoneInfo tokyo = TimeZoneInfo.CreateCustomTimeZone( "Test/Tokyo", TimeSpan.FromHours(9), "Test JST", "Test JST"); timeSystem.TimeProvider.LocalTimeZone = tokyo; DateTime now = timeSystem.DateTime.Now; // 2026-01-15 09:00 (JST) DateTimeOffset offsetNow = timeSystem.DateTimeOffset.Now; // offset +09:00 TimeZoneInfo local = timeSystem.TimeZoneInfo.Local; // Test/Tokyo // RegisterTimeZone adds zones resolvable via FindSystemTimeZoneById / GetSystemTimeZones timeSystem.TimeProvider.RegisterTimeZone(tokyo); TimeZoneInfo resolved = timeSystem.TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById("Test/Tokyo"); The registry is seeded from the host's TimeZoneInfo.GetSystemTimeZones(), so well-known ids keep resolving; setting LocalTimeZone registers that zone automatically.

Implement ITimeProvider directly when you need something more interesting than a single DateTime, for example a clock that ticks per virtual thread. See Thread-aware time provider for a worked example. Wrap your provider in a factory and pass it in: ITimeProviderFactory factory = new GalleryClockFactory(...); MockTimeSystem timeSystem = new(factory); ITimeProviderFactory receives a callback that your provider must invoke whenever the simulated time changes; the notifications and waiting timers depend on it. timeSystem.TimeProvider returns your provider itself. When you move its clock directly, the timers that became due fire afterward, as the clock is already past them. The waits of the MockTimeSystem, e.g. Task.Delay or Thread.Sleep, still fire them in order.

Pass an existing MockTimeSystem into a MockFileSystem so file-system timestamps and time-related assertions stay consistent: MockTimeSystem timeSystem = new(new DateTime(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc)); MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(o => o.UseTimeSystem(timeSystem)); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("catalog.json", "[]"); DateTime created = fileSystem.File.GetCreationTimeUtc("catalog.json"); // created is anchored to 2026-01-01

.NET 8 or later ToTimeProvider() needs System.TimeProvider, which exists on .NET 8 or later. Code that depends on the built-in System.TimeProvider instead of ITimeSystem can run against the same mock: ToTimeProvider() wraps any ITimeSystem as a TimeProvider. On a MockTimeSystem, the simulated clock is visible through GetUtcNow() and GetTimestamp(), and the timers that the TimeProvider creates run on the mock's timers. MockTimeSystem timeSystem = new(new DateTime(2026, 1, 15, 10, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc)); TimeProvider timeProvider = timeSystem.ToTimeProvider(); timeSystem.TimeProvider.AdvanceBy(TimeSpan.FromHours(2)); await That(timeProvider.GetUtcNow()).IsEqualTo(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 1, 15, 12, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero)); A timer created through the TimeProvider keeps firing when its callback throws, like a real timer, regardless of the TimerStrategy configured on the MockTimeSystem.

MockTimeSystem.On lets a test observe time-related events from the system under test, which is useful for asserting "the code asked to sleep for 5 seconds" without relying on side effects. MockTimeSystem timeSystem = new(); using IAwaitableCallback<TimeSpan> sleeps = timeSystem.On.ThreadSleep(); new Gallery(timeSystem).CloseForTheNight(); // waits 5 seconds before switching off the lights TimeSpan[] requestedSleeps = sleeps.Wait(count: 1); await That(requestedSleeps[0]).IsEqualTo(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5)); Like the file-system notifications, each method returns an IAwaitableCallback<T> you dispose to unsubscribe and Wait/WaitAsync to block until enough events arrive.

Method on On Fires when T DateTimeRead() DateTime.Now, UtcNow or Today is read DateTime DateTimeOffsetRead() DateTimeOffset.Now or UtcNow is read DateTimeOffset TaskDelay() Task.Delay (any overload) is called TimeSpan ThreadSleep() Thread.Sleep (any overload) is called TimeSpan TimeChanged() the simulated time advanced (auto-advance or manual) DateTime PeriodicTimer.WaitingForNextTick() a PeriodicTimer is waiting for its next tick (.NET 8 or later) IPeriodicTimer Each accepts an optional callback (run synchronously when the event fires) and an optional predicate to filter events before they are recorded. // Only record sleeps longer than 1 second using IAwaitableCallback<TimeSpan> longSleeps = timeSystem.On.ThreadSleep( predicate: ts => ts > TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1));

MockTimeSystem.PeriodicTimer wraps System.Threading.PeriodicTimer (IPeriodicTimer). It's the async pull-based counterpart to Timer: instead of registering a callback and waiting for it to fire, your code awaits WaitForNextTickAsync() inside a loop. .NET 8 or later ITimeSystem.PeriodicTimer is only available on .NET 8 and later. Typical use case: a hosted/background service that does work on a fixed cadence and needs to be testable without actually waiting that long, like a night guard who walks a round through the gallery every 30 minutes: NightGuard.cs public class NightGuard(ITimeSystem timeSystem, IFileSystem fileSystem) { public async Task PatrolAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken) { using IPeriodicTimer timer = timeSystem.PeriodicTimer.New(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(30)); while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(cancellationToken)) { fileSystem.File.AppendAllText("guard-rounds.log", $"{timeSystem.DateTime.UtcNow:o}\n"); } } }

To assert exactly how often the loop ran, turn auto-advance off and advance the clock by hand. WaitForNextTickAsync then stays pending until the simulated time reaches the next tick. On.PeriodicTimer.WaitingForNextTick() fires every time the guard calls WaitForNextTickAsync, so waiting for it tells the test that the guard finished the previous round and is waiting for the next one: MockTimeSystem timeSystem = new(o => o.DisableAutoAdvance()); MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(o => o.UseTimeSystem(timeSystem)); NightGuard guard = new(timeSystem, fileSystem); using CancellationTokenSource cts = new(); using IAwaitableCallback<IPeriodicTimer> waiting = timeSystem.On.PeriodicTimer.WaitingForNextTick(); Task patrol = guard.PatrolAsync(cts.Token); // The guard is waiting for the first round; nothing was logged yet waiting.Wait(); await That(fileSystem.File.Exists("guard-rounds.log")).IsFalse(); timeSystem.TimeProvider.AdvanceBy(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(30)); waiting.Wait(); await That(fileSystem.File.ReadAllLines("guard-rounds.log")).HasCount(1); cts.Cancel(); await That(async () => await patrol).Throws<OperationCanceledException>(); Like the real PeriodicTimer, advancing the clock by several periods at once results in a single tick, not one tick per elapsed period. WaitingForNextTick accepts an optional predicate to filter, which is useful when multiple periodic timers run in the same test and you only want to wait for one specific period.

documents.t: With auto-advance on (the default), every WaitForNextTickAsync returns immediately and advances the simulated clock by one Period, so the loop runs as fast as it can until it is cancelled. That is useful to check that the loop does its work, but not to count iterations: MockTimeSystem timeSystem = new(); MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(o => o.UseTimeSystem(timeSystem)); NightGuard guard = new(timeSystem, fileSystem); using CancellationTokenSource cts = new(); using IAwaitableCallback<IPeriodicTimer> waiting = timeSystem.On.PeriodicTimer.WaitingForNextTick(); Task patrol = guard.PatrolAsync(cts.Token); waiting.Wait(count: 5); // the guard finished at least four rounds cts.Cancel(); await That(async () => await patrol).Throws<OperationCanceledException>(); await That(fileSystem.File.ReadAllLines("guard-rounds.log").Length) .IsGreaterThanOrEqualTo(4);

IPeriodicTimer.Period is settable; the next WaitForNextTickAsync uses the new value: using IPeriodicTimer timer = timeSystem.PeriodicTimer.New(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)); await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(); // waits 1s timer.Period = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100); await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(); // waits 100ms Periods below 1 ms throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException, matching the base class library (BCL).

Dispose() ends the loop the next time around: WaitForNextTickAsync returns false instead of true, so the while (await …) exits cleanly. A CancellationToken passed into WaitForNextTickAsync makes it throw an OperationCanceledException when triggered. // graceful: dispose ends the loop on the next tick timer.Dispose(); // abrupt: cancellation throws inside the await cts.Cancel();

MockTimeSystem.Stopwatch wraps System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch. It exposes both the instance API (IStopwatch: Start, Stop, Elapsed, ElapsedMilliseconds, ElapsedTicks, Restart, Reset, IsRunning) and the static API on the factory itself (IStopwatchFactory: Frequency, IsHighResolution, GetTimestamp, StartNew).

ITimeSystem timeSystem = new MockTimeSystem(); IStopwatch sw = timeSystem.Stopwatch.StartNew(); // Simulate work that takes 5 seconds; Sleep auto-advances the simulated clock timeSystem.Thread.Sleep(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5)); sw.Stop(); await That(sw.Elapsed).IsEqualTo(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));

A real Stopwatch reads the OS monotonic clock: it measures elapsed real time, completely independent of the wall-clock date. Setting the system clock backwards mid-measurement doesn't subtract from Elapsed; only actual time passing does. MockTimeSystem mirrors that distinction. The two knobs on TimeProvider behave differently: Method DateTime.UtcNow Running Stopwatch.Elapsed AdvanceBy(TimeSpan) Moves forward by the span Moves forward by the span SetTo(DateTime) Jumps to the given instant Unchanged MockTimeSystem timeSystem = new(new DateTime(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc)); IStopwatch sw = timeSystem.Stopwatch.StartNew(); // Jump the wall clock backwards by a year; Stopwatch is unaffected timeSystem.TimeProvider.SetTo(new DateTime(2025, 1, 1)); await That(sw.Elapsed).IsEqualTo(TimeSpan.Zero); // AdvanceBy moves both the wall clock and the monotonic clock timeSystem.TimeProvider.AdvanceBy(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5)); await That(sw.Elapsed).IsEqualTo(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5)); This means tests that mix Stopwatch measurements with manual SetTo calls (e.g. simulating a clock change at midnight, NTP correction, daylight-saving switch) don't produce nonsensical elapsed values. The Stopwatch always reflects "real" simulated elapsed time. The same monotonic clock backs Timer, PeriodicTimer and Task.Delay; none of them are affected by SetTo either.

The static surface lives on the factory (timeSystem.Stopwatch), not on individual IStopwatch instances: long t1 = timeSystem.Stopwatch.GetTimestamp(); timeSystem.Thread.Sleep(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2)); long t2 = timeSystem.Stopwatch.GetTimestamp(); double seconds = (t2 - t1) / (double)timeSystem.Stopwatch.Frequency; // 2.0 On .NET 8+, GetElapsedTime does the math for you: long start = timeSystem.Stopwatch.GetTimestamp(); timeSystem.Thread.Sleep(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2)); TimeSpan elapsed = timeSystem.Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(start); // 00:00:02 TimeSpan span = timeSystem.Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(t1, t2); // 00:00:02 On the mock, Frequency is fixed at TimeSpan.TicksPerSecond * 10 = 100,000,000 (100 MHz, i.e. 10 ns per timestamp tick) and IsHighResolution is always true. The real Stopwatch.Frequency varies by hardware and OS; the mock pins it to a stable value so timestamp arithmetic in tests is deterministic.

Start/Stop/Reset/Restart behave exactly as on the BCL: IStopwatch sw = timeSystem.Stopwatch.StartNew(); timeSystem.Thread.Sleep(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3)); sw.Stop(); // Elapsed = 3s timeSystem.Thread.Sleep(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10)); // paused, ignored sw.Start(); // resume timeSystem.Thread.Sleep(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2)); await That(sw.Elapsed).IsEqualTo(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5)); sw.Restart(); // Elapsed = 0, running sw.Reset(); // Elapsed = 0, stopped A second Start() on an already-running stopwatch is a no-op, matching the BCL.

By default, all threads share one simulated clock. Two parallel threads each calling Sleep(5s) therefore advance it by 10 seconds total, which doesn't match what would happen in the real world (where they'd both finish after roughly 5 seconds of wall time). The fix is a custom ITimeProvider that stores the clock per logical thread using AsyncLocal<DateTime>. The library does not ship one; copy and adapt the example below.

ThreadAwareTimeProvider public sealed class ThreadAwareTimeProvider : ITimeProvider { private static readonly AsyncLocal<DateTime> Now = new(); private static readonly AsyncLocal<DateTime?> SynchronizedTime = new(); private DateTime? _synchronizedTime; public ThreadAwareTimeProvider(DateTime? now = null) { Now.Value = now ?? DateTime.Now; } public DateTime Read() { CheckSynchronization(); return Now.Value; } public void AdvanceBy(TimeSpan interval) { CheckSynchronization(); Now.Value = Now.Value.Add(interval); } public void SetTo(DateTime value) => Now.Value = value; /// Aligns every async context to the value of the calling context on next read. public void SynchronizeClock() => _synchronizedTime = Now.Value; private void CheckSynchronization() { if (_synchronizedTime is { } target && SynchronizedTime.Value != target) { SynchronizedTime.Value = target; Now.Value = target; } } // The remaining ITimeProvider members are boilerplate and omitted here. } AsyncLocal<T> flows with the async context, so each Task.Run (or new Thread) starts with its own copy of the current time. SynchronizeClock() lets you re-merge the per-thread clocks when you need to compare them.

With this provider, parallel tasks advance their own clocks independently: task i ticks by i seconds per step: ThreadAwareTimeProvider timeProvider = new(); MockTimeSystem timeSystem = new(timeProvider); DateTime start = timeSystem.DateTime.UtcNow; ConcurrentDictionary<int, List<int>> delays = new(); for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) { int id = i; TimeSpan step = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(id); await Task.Run(async () => { for (int j = 0; j < 20; j++) { await timeSystem.Task.Delay(step); int ms = (int)(timeSystem.DateTime.UtcNow - start).TotalMilliseconds; delays.AddOrUpdate(id, _ => new List<int> { ms }, (_, l) => { l.Add(ms); return l; }); } }); } // Task 1's clock advanced 1s per step → [1000, 2000, …, 20000] // Task 5's clock advanced 5s per step → [5000, 10000, …, 100000] await That(delays[1]).IsEqualTo(Enumerable.Range(1, 20).Select(x => x * 1000)); await That(delays[5]).IsEqualTo(Enumerable.Range(1, 20).Select(x => x * 5000)); The same pattern works with raw Threads: AsyncLocal<T> flows across both.

When a parallel branch finishes and you want subsequent reads on the main thread to continue from its clock, call SynchronizeClock() before joining: ThreadAwareTimeProvider timeProvider = new(); MockTimeSystem timeSystem = new(timeProvider); DateTime start = timeSystem.DateTime.UtcNow; await timeSystem.Task.Delay(1_000); // main: +1s await Task.Run(async () => { await timeSystem.Task.Delay(1_000); // task: starts from +1s, now at +2s timeProvider.SynchronizeClock(); // publish +2s as the new baseline }); timeSystem.TimeProvider.AdvanceBy(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(1_000)); // Without SynchronizeClock the main thread would be at +2s (its own +1s, plus the +1s above). // With it, the main thread picks up the task's +2s and ends at +3s. await That((int)(timeSystem.DateTime.UtcNow - start).TotalMilliseconds).IsEqualTo(3_000);

MockTimeSystem.Timer wraps System.Threading.Timer (ITimer). The mocked timer lets you wait for a specific number of executions instead of sleeping. For the await-based pull loop variant, see PeriodicTimer.

MockTimeSystem.Timer.New(...) returns the production ITimer interface, but the underlying instance is always an ITimerMock on a MockTimeSystem. Cast it once to gain the testing-only Wait method (or fetch the mock later from timeSystem.TimerHandler[index] if the system under test owns the timer): MockTimeSystem timeSystem = new(); int ticks = 0; ITimerMock timer = (ITimerMock)timeSystem.Timer.New(_ => ticks++, state: null, dueTime: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), period: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)); // Block until the timer fired 3 times (or throw TimeoutException) timer.Wait(executionCount: 3); await That(ticks).IsEqualTo(3); ITimerMock.Wait(int executionCount = 1, int timeout = 10000, Action<ITimerMock>? callback = null) is the testing-only addition. Note timeout is milliseconds (not TimeSpan; this differs from IAwaitableCallback<T>.Wait, which takes a TimeSpan?). The optional callback runs between executions and receives the timer itself; call Dispose() on it to stop early.

documents.t: WithTimerStrategy(TimerStrategy) controls when timers start and how exceptions inside callbacks are handled: MockTimeSystem timeSystem = new(); timeSystem.WithTimerStrategy(new TimerStrategy( mode: TimerMode.StartOnMockWait, swallowExceptions: true)); TimerMode Behavior StartImmediately Default. Timer thread starts as soon as the timer is constructed, matching the real Timer. StartOnMockWait Timer is dormant until ITimerMock.Wait(...) is called. Removes thread-scheduling races from the test. SwallowExceptions Behavior false (default) An exception in the callback throws: your test sees it, mirroring the real-world process crash. true Exceptions are silently dropped, matching legacy code that handled them in unspecified ways.
